query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tailored refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) interlayer designed via composition tuning (for example, incorporating elements such as tungsten, tantalum, and molybdenum) will effectively bridge the thermo-mechanical mismatch between tungsten and CuCrZr. This interlayer is expected to reduce thermal stresses, inhibit brittle intermetallic formation, and improve the durability of the bonding interface under fusion reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Direct bonding between tungsten and CuCrZr, which is susceptible to brittleness and thermal expansion mismatch leading to interfacial failures.
generation.intervention: Introduce a compositionally optimized RHEA interlayer between W and CuCrZr by adjusting the elemental mix (e.g., adding Ta and Mo) to achieve intermediate thermal expansion and high thermal conductivity.
generation.conditions: Extreme operational conditions typical of nuclear fusion reactors, including high heat flux, intense neutron irradiation, and frequent thermal cycling.
generation.structural_mediator: The RHEA interlayer mediates between the disparate properties of W and CuCrZr by providing an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and robust thermal conductivity, while also offering enhanced radiation tolerance.
generation.mechanism: The optimized RHEA composition minimizes stress concentration by moderating thermal expansion differences and prevents the formation of brittle intermetallic compounds through controlled phase stability, thereby enhancing mechanical integrity at the interface.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced formation of brittle intermetallic phases, improved mechanical bonding, and longer component lifetime due to better accommodation of thermal stresses and radiation effects across the interface.
generation.baseline: Conventional direct bonding between W and CuCrZr, which often fails due to significant thermal expansion mismatch and the formation of brittle compounds under reactor conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the RHEA interlayer is dependent on achieving precise compositional control; deviations in the alloy composition or prolonged exposure to extreme irradiation may limit its performance.
generation.uncertainty: While the direction of the effect is expected to be beneficial, the optimal composition and long-term stability of the RHEA interlayer under continuous fusion reactor conditions remain to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of bonded joints where tungsten and CuCrZr are connected via the tailored RHEA interlayer, alongside control samples with direct bonding. Subject both sets to accelerated testing involving cyclic thermal loads, high heat flux, and simulated neutron irradiation representative of fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (SEM/TEM) to monitor phase formation and intermetallic compounds
Thermal expansion measurements across the interface
Irradiation damage analysis (defect densities and grain stability)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the joints incorporating the RHEA interlayer do not show statistically significant improvements in interfacial strength, reduced brittle phase formation, and better accommodation of thermal expansion mismatch compared to directly bonded W-CuCrZr samples.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials [32] . Two main suggested mechanisms are discussed in the literature: (i) defect clusters produced during irradiation can migrate to sub-grain boundaries and form cell structures that lead to small grain formation [32] and (ii) cascades that are larger than the grain size can form stacking faults across the grain breaking it into two separate crystalline structures (observed in FCC material) [33] . decision.trend: Earlier research in fusion‐relevant materials started with direct bonding of tungsten to copper alloys, which encountered severe issues such as brittle intermetallic formation and thermal‐stress–induced failures. In parallel, multiple groups began to explore refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) processed by techniques like magnetron sputtering and laser powder bed fusion. These studies focused on achieving microstructural stability, optimizing grain sizes, and improving radiation tolerance. Although these efforts have significantly advanced the field by controlling phases and enabling conformal microstructures under extreme irradiation and thermal cycling, the critical gap of designing an interlayer with intermediate thermo‐mechanical properties remains.
decision.unsolved: The main unsolved issue is finding or engineering an interlayer material that can bridge the significant mismatch in thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, and radiation response between tungsten and CuCrZr while preventing the formation of brittle intermetallic phases.
decision.lever: Develop a tailored refractory high‐entropy alloy interlayer—by selecting and optimizing a composition (for example, incorporating elements such as tungsten, tantalum, and molybdenum) that yields an intermediate coefficient of thermal expansion and robust thermal conductivity as well as high radiation tolerance.
decision.why: The trend shows that progressively engineered compositions (via precise alloy design) in RHEAs provide enhanced behavior under extreme reactor conditions. A compositionally optimized interlayer naturally follows as the next step to resolve the thermal and mechanical mismatches at the tungsten/CuCrZr interface, as indicated by previous successes using similar refractory alloys in fusion‐relevant applications.
